children.name: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
children.blurb: Drafting proposals from past work covers the practice of turning an organization's completed projects, publications, reports, and prior applications into new grant proposal text.

children.name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
children.blurb: Funder formatting and compliance covers the mechanical and administrative requirements that a grant proposal must meet before a funding body will review it.

children.name: Budgets and Allowable Costs
children.blurb: Budgets and allowable costs in AI research grant proposals cover the direct and indirect expenses a funder will reimburse, including personnel, equipment, data acquisition, cloud compute, and institutional overhead.

children.name: Finding Collaborators
children.blurb: Finding collaborators in grant proposals and funding means identifying researchers whose expertise, data, or institutional role can strengthen a proposal.

children.blurb: Predicting proposal success uses machine learning to estimate the likelihood that a grant application will be funded, based on proposal text, applicant history, funder priorities, and past review patterns.

sections.body: Grant proposals and funding work in AI now means using language models to turn prior research into draft sections, checking submissions against agency formatting rules, estimating budgets against allowable cost lists, matching potential collaborators by publication and grant history, and scoring proposals against past award data. These are not theoretical capabilities, they are routine parts of many research workflows. The site's library of 135 research papers and 11222 extracted claims provides a concrete base for drafting from past work. Tools in this space read a researcher's own papers and pull out aims, methods, and expected outcomes into proposal language. They also compare a draft to a funder's page limits, required sections, and citation formats.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The solved parts are narrow. Drafting from past work reliably produces summaries and background sections, but it cannot invent a novel research plan or argue why a project matters. Compliance checking catches missing sections, wrong margins, and disallowed fonts, but it does not understand an agency's shifting priorities. Budget tools flag costs that exceed a stated cap or fall outside a category, yet they cannot judge whether a budget is realistic for the proposed work. Collaborator matching finds people with overlapping keywords or co-authorship networks, but it misses working style, availability, and institutional politics. Predicting proposal success remains the weakest area, because reviewer scores and program fit are not captured in public data, so any score is a rough guess.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Drafting Proposals from Past Work to turn existing papers into a first draft, then move to Funder Formatting and Compliance to make that draft match the agency's required structure. Budgets and Allowable Costs handles the financial side, checking each line against the funder's rules before submission. Finding Collaborators helps build the team by searching for researchers whose past work fits the proposal's aims. Predicting Proposal Success sits at the end, offering a rough check on whether the assembled proposal is likely to be funded.
